tldr: A benchmark study that profiles 18 open VLA models broken down into 7 stages on edge hardware (NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor and AMD Ryzen AI Max+). It reveals that inference latency is determined not by model parameter size but by the action generation iteration method, and that optimizing GPU kernels turns memory bandwidth and host CPU preprocessing into the new bottlenecks.
overview:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models, which directly predict robot action commands from visual and language inputs, are drawing significant attention as a key breakthrough for general-purpose robot control. However, controlling real-world robots is a constant battle against a changing physical environment. If model inference is slow, the scene changes before actions can be executed, leading to control failure. Considering safety, privacy, and communication latency, inference must be performed in real time directly on edge devices onboard the robot.

Yet, existing benchmarks have predominantly reported only task success rates, splitting the inference call into at most three broad phases. As a result, it remained entirely unclear which operations are the true bottlenecks on real hardware, and how much optimizations like quantization and specialized inference runtimes actually help.

To address this, the authors built "VLA-HWBench," a benchmark that breaks down the full inference call into seven fine-grained stages—from CPU preprocessing to GPU computation—across 18 open VLA models (19 configurations). Across two modern edge platforms with distinct architectures (an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor and an AMD Ryzen AI Max+ PRO 395), they rigorously profiled inference while systematically applying optimizations such as compilation and low-bit quantization.

The findings show that the primary driver of latency variance is not model size, but the number of iterations in action generation. Furthermore, as GPU execution is optimized, host CPU preprocessing emerges as a major bottleneck accounting for up to 40% of runtime, and for fully optimized models, memory bandwidth becomes the ultimate physical limit. This study provides highly practical guidelines for the future design of VLAs for robotics.
contributions: Built VLA-HWBench, a benchmark measuring inference latency on edge hardware across 18 open VLA models covering four representative action generation paradigms.
Decomposed the inference pipeline from host observation ingestion to action output into seven stages, cleanly isolating CPU preprocessing and kernel-level execution times.

Demonstrated that latency variance is governed not by parameter count (explaining 15% or less of the variance), but by the number of iterations in action generation (token-by-token decoding vs. parallel or flow-matching).

Systematically evaluated optimizations like kernel fusion and 4-bit quantization, revealing how CPU preprocessing (Python overhead, thread wakeups) and memory bandwidth emerge as the new bottlenecks as GPU execution speeds up.

sections.heading: Where Does the Time Go When Running VLA Models on Edge Hardware?
sections.summary: Closed-loop robot control demands low-latency edge inference, yet prior work evaluated few models with coarse profiling, leaving true bottlenecks unknown. This work proposes VLA-HWBench, a 7-stage benchmark answering three questions on latency drivers, optimization effects, and hardware limits.
sections.details:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models offer an innovative paradigm by directly generating robot joint commands from camera images and natural language instructions. However, inference latency is fatal in robot control. If inference takes too long, obstacles or targets move while the robot executes previous commands, making observation data stale and causing task failure. Considering potential connection dropouts and privacy concerns, self-contained inference onboard robot edge devices is essential.

Yet, the behavior of recent VLA models on edge hardware has not been systematically studied. Prior work suffered from three major gaps. First, they did not broadly compare the diverse ways actions are generated (flow-matching denoising, single-pass parallel decoding, autoregressive token generation like LLMs, or reasoning before acting). Second, they split an inference call into at most three phases, ignoring time spent on CPU image preprocessing or host-device data transfers. Third, they did not compare optimizations like compilation and low-bit quantization across models under identical conditions.

To solve this, the authors developed VLA-HWBench, combining 18 open models and two cutting-edge edge SoCs (an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor and an AMD Ryzen AI Max+ PRO 395). By dissecting the inference pipeline into seven stages and measuring them accurately, the study resolves three core questions: what determines latency (Q1), how much optimizations help and where time moves (Q2), and what bottlenecks remain after optimization (Q3).

sections.heading: Diverse Action Generation and What Prior Edge Benchmarks Missed
sections.summary: Prior research primarily focused on evaluating VLA task success rates, while hardware profiling remained limited to a handful of models or select components. Additionally, the effects of inference runtimes and quantization were only evaluated piecemeal on isolated models.
sections.details:
Recent VLA models employ diverse approaches to generate actions. These include flow-matching, which integrates action trajectories over a fixed number of steps; parallel decoding, which outputs all actions in a single pass; autoregressive models, which predict action tokens one by one like traditional LLMs; and reasoning models, which generate thought plans before acting. While these paradigms have been compared by task success rates, the computational cost each incurs on edge hardware has remained unclear.

Prior studies on edge VLA inference (such as Taherin et al. and Zhou et al.) examined at most around five models, and their measurements focused narrowly on specific GPU components like action experts. Moreover, while dedicated inference runtimes (TensorRT, FlashRT), quantization techniques (FP8, 4-bit NVFP4), and real-time chunking schemes have been proposed, they have only been evaluated piecemeal on individual models.

VLA-HWBench serves as the first comprehensive framework to cover these diverse action generation paradigms, using identical observation data and strict stage boundaries to fairly evaluate the contributions of inference optimizations.

sections.heading: Dissecting Inference into Seven Stages: Formulation and Design Principles
sections.summary: The entire inference call is split and formulated across seven stages from CPU preprocessing to GPU execution and postprocessing. Using the 50 ms robot control cycle as a deadline, roofline models diagnose hardware and software limits.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Research Questions and Pipeline Formulation
A VLA model receives camera images, robot proprioception (joint angles, etc.), and language instructions, and outputs an action chunk of $H$ steps executed by the robot controller. In this benchmark, the total inference time $T$ from receiving observation data on the host to outputting actions is formulated as the sum of seven stages (S0 through S6):
- S0: CPU preprocessing (image resizing, normalization, etc.)
- S1: Host-to-device data transfer (memory copies from CPU to GPU)
- S2: Vision encoding (extracting image features via the vision tower)
- S3: Language model prefill (processing prompt tokens and building KV cache)
- S4: Action generation (executing the action head)
- S5: CPU postprocessing (tensor formatting, etc.)
- S6: Residual overhead (Python dispatch, etc.)

In particular, action generation (S4) is represented as the product of the number of iterations $N$ and the cost per iteration $t$ ($N \times t$), directly corresponding to the number of denoising steps in flow-matching or the number of generated tokens in autoregressive models.

### 3.2 Evaluation Metrics
Clear metrics are defined for the three research questions. For Q1 (where time goes), the stage breakdowns and latency per action ($T/H$) are calculated. Standard benchmark LIBERO operates its control loop at 20 Hz (a 50 ms period), meaning models must achieve $T/H < 50$ ms to keep up with real-time control. For Q2 (optimization effects), speedup over reference configurations and output action fidelity (cosine similarity) are tracked. For Q3 (bottlenecks), roofline models using floating-point operations $F$ and weight memory reads $W$ determine whether each GPU stage is compute-bound or memory bandwidth-bound.

### 3.3 Design Principles
To ensure fair comparisons, the benchmark adopts the same library configurations as each model's official LIBERO evaluation code, applying optimizations step by step from an unoptimized "reference" setup. Stage times are isolated even inside CUDA graphs by analyzing kernel call order and repetitive patterns. Furthermore, comparing an Arm CPU-based Jetson and an x86 CPU-based AMD platform allows isolating the effects of host CPUs and GPU architectures.

sections.heading: 18 Models and 2 Edge SoCs: Concrete Experimental Setup
sections.summary: 18 popular open VLA models from Hugging Face were selected and evaluated on the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor and AMD Ryzen AI Max+ PRO 395. All models were fed identical LIBERO-10 observations and measured with synchronized hardware timers.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Model Coverage
18 popular open VLA models released between 2025 and 2026 with available LIBERO evaluation code and checkpoints were selected. They cover four major action generation paradigms. Because MolmoAct2 includes both a flow head and a discrete token head, a total of 19 reference configurations were tested.

### 4.2 Inference Runtimes and Optimization Hierarchy
Models were run on four inference backends:
- LeRobot: Hugging Face's robotics library, based on PyTorch with torch.compile support.
- Authors' code: The reference eager PyTorch implementation released with each model.
- FlashRT: A dedicated inference runtime for VLAs supporting kernel fusion, CUDA graphs, and FP8/NVFP4 quantization.
- TensorRT: NVIDIA's compiler-based inference engine.
For Q1, all models were evaluated in their unoptimized reference environments. For Q2, representative models supporting the full stack of optimizations ($\pi_{0.5}$ and GR00T N1.7) were used to systematically evaluate compilation, specialized runtimes, and low-bit quantization.

### 4.3 Hardware Platforms
Two modern edge platforms were evaluated: the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor (14-core Arm Neoverse-V3AE CPU, Blackwell architecture GPU, 273 GB/s memory bandwidth) and the AMD Ryzen AI Max+ PRO 395 (16-core x86 Zen 5 CPU, RDNA 3.5 architecture GPU, 246 GB/s memory bandwidth). While both feature unified memory, their peak compute capabilities and CPU characteristics differ significantly.

### 4.4 Measurement Protocol and Profiling
All configurations were supplied with identical real LIBERO-10 observation data (two $256\times 256$ camera images, robot state, and instruction text). After 20 warmup calls, the median of up to 100 runs was recorded using explicit device synchronization. Variations across 24 different frames within an episode were also evaluated. GPU profilers categorized kernels (e.g., matrix-unit usage vs. non-matrix), while CPU profiling tracked thread scaling and core C-state (idle power state) transitions.

sections.heading: Experimental Results: The Fall of the Parameter Myth and the True Bottlenecks
sections.summary: Latency is driven by action iterations rather than model size, spanning up to a 157x gap. Dedicated backends and 4-bit weights yield up to 7x speedups, but optimizing GPU execution causes CPU preprocessing to consume up to 40% of runtime.
sections.details:
### 5.1 [Q1] Where Does the Time Go? Drivers of Latency
In the reference configurations on the Jetson, action generation (S4) was the largest stage in 14 of 19 configurations, taking 42% to 99% of total runtime. Latency varied dramatically, spanning an 82x range on the Jetson (77 ms for X-VLA to 6.3 s for VLA-0) and a 157x range on AMD (114 ms to 17.9 s). Only 10 configurations on the Jetson and 9 on AMD satisfied the 50 ms/action control deadline.

Crucially, model size (parameter count) showed almost no correlation with latency. Linear regression between log parameters and log latency yielded an $R^2$ of only 9% on the Jetson and 15% on AMD. For example, GR00T N1.7 (3.1B) and VLA-0 (3.8B) have similar parameter counts, but VLA-0 was 53x slower on the Jetson.

This gap is governed by the number of action generation iterations ($N$). Flow-matching models require only a few steps and parallel decoding models take just one pass, whereas autoregressive models sequentially run dozens to hundreds of language model forward passes per action. Generating 208 tokens consumed 99% of VLA-0's total call time. Similarly, reasoning models spent roughly 90% of their time generating thought tokens.

### 5.2 [Q2] How Much Do Optimizations Help, and Where Does the Time Move?
Progressive optimization of $\pi_{0.5}$ and GR00T N1.7 on the Jetson reduced runtime from 318 ms to 44 ms (a 7.2x speedup) for $\pi_{0.5}$, and from 119 ms to 46 ms (a 2.6x speedup) for GR00T N1.7. FlashRT, combining kernel fusion with NVFP4 (4-bit weights), was the biggest contributor, running 2.6x to 2.9x faster than PyTorch with torch.compile alone.

However, optimization shifted the bottlenecks across the pipeline. As GPU computation shrunk drastically, the share of unshortened stages surged. For GR00T N1.7, CPU preprocessing accounted for only 12% initially, but grew into the dominant bottleneck at 39% of total call time after optimization.

### 5.3 [Q3] What Limits Latency After Optimization?
Roofline analysis of fully optimized configurations revealed that no single resource acts as a universal bottleneck:
- Action generation (S4): Because each denoising step processes very few tokens (10 to 41 tokens), computational intensity is low, making it strictly memory bandwidth-bound. FlashRT on the Jetson already reads weights at near 75% of peak memory bandwidth, reaching physical hardware limits.
- Vision encoding (S2) and Prefill (S3): Processing large token counts should make these stages compute-bound. However, due to unfused kernels and lack of low-precision support, they achieve only 6% to 42% of peak hardware performance (limited by software).
- CPU preprocessing (S0): The 39% share in optimized GR00T stemmed from serial Python execution combined with the overhead of waking 14 PyTorch worker threads that entered deep C-states (power-saving idle) during GPU work. On AMD's faster single-core x86 CPU, this preprocessing finished 5x faster, underscoring the critical role of host CPU single-thread performance.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Architectural Directions for Edge VLA Design
sections.summary: Achieving real-time VLA inference requires reducing iteration count rather than simply shrinking model parameters. Selecting edge hardware with ample memory bandwidth and a fast host CPU is equally essential.
sections.details:
This study presented VLA-HWBench, comprehensively profiling the inference latency of VLA models on edge hardware and dissecting the mechanics of edge execution.

Based on these findings, three clear architectural directions are proposed:
1. Model Design: Rather than blindly pruning parameter counts, architects should prioritize reducing action generation iterations. Minimizing flow-matching steps or adopting parallel decoding is the fastest route to low latency.
2. Software Development: Kernel fusion and 4-bit low-precision quantization must be extended to more models and platforms like AMD. Furthermore, host CPU data preprocessing must be aggressively optimized and rewritten in C++.
3. Hardware Selection: For edge SoCs, memory bandwidth and host CPU speed matter far more for closed-loop robot control than peak GPU compute figures (TFLOPS).

sections.heading: Appendix: Frame-to-Frame Latency Jitter, Action Fidelity, and Measurement Nuances
sections.summary: Details show that reasoning models experience up to 122% latency swings across frames, and compilation and quantization carry the risk of flipping discrete gripper commands.
sections.details:
The appendix provides detailed experimental analyses omitted from the main text.

### Latency Variance Across Frames (Input Sensitivity)
Measuring latency across a full 24-frame robot episode revealed that models with fixed token counts experienced variance within a few percent. However, reasoning models (such as DeepThinkVLA and MolmoAct2-Think), whose thought token counts fluctuate based on scene complexity, showed severe latency swings between 12% and 122% across frames. In real-time closed-loop control, unpredictable spikes in inference time pose a major risk of control instability.

### Action Fidelity Under Optimization
While compilation and quantization accelerate inference, output action fidelity must be verified. FP8 quantization maintained high cosine similarity above 0.998 against FP16 outputs, and NVFP4 stayed above 0.93. However, compiler reordering of operations caused sign flips in discrete gripper open/close commands in $\pi_{0.5}$. When adopting edge optimizations, verifying task success rates and control commands is just as crucial as tracking latency gains.

takeaways: To speed up VLA inference, prioritize reducing action generation iterations (lowering denoising steps or using parallel decoding) over simply shrinking model parameter counts.

No matter how fast GPU kernels become, Python image preprocessing and thread management emerge as the dominant bottleneck, making host CPU pipeline optimization (C++ rewrites, single-thread speed) essential.
Because fully optimized edge VLAs run up against memory bandwidth limits, hardware selection should prioritize memory bandwidth (GB/s) and host CPU performance over nominal GPU TFLOPS.
Compilation and low-bit quantization (FP8/NVFP4) deliver multi-fold speedups, but action command fidelity—such as gripper command sign flips—must be rigorously verified.
limitations: Evaluations are based on LIBERO-10 simulation inputs (e.g., two 256x256 camera images); real-world robotic setups requiring higher resolutions or more camera views may see vision encoding consume a much larger share of latency.

Advanced inference optimization runtimes like FlashRT and TensorRT are currently available only for specific models ($\pi_{0.5}$ and GR00T) and exclusively on NVIDIA platforms, limiting cross-model optimization comparisons.
While cosine similarity and action errors were evaluated, closed-loop task success rates on physical robots under optimized and low-bit quantized models were outside the scope of this paper.
